C.O.A.D is a team of passionate college students from Government Engineering College, Thrissur, driven by curiosity, creativity, and a love for building. For us, the NASA Space Apps Challenge is an opportunity to push boundaries, experiment boldly, collaborate, and transform imagination into innovation.

summary: Field Shift is a decision-support tool that helps rainfed farmers and extension advisers in Solapur, Maharashtra, explore crop-rotation options under uncertain monsoons. Using 41 years (1985–2025) of NASA POWER daily weather (MERRA-2 and CERES-derived rainfall, temperature, humidity, wind and solar radiation), it runs an FAO-56 daily soil-water balance for three rotations on shallow, medium and deep black soils: fallow then rabi sorghum, sole pigeon pea, and pearl millet then chickpea. Instead of a single winning answer, it shows how much water stress each rotation faces in typical and bad years, how often the planting window is missed, and how stable each comparison is across 500 plausible parameter combinations. Parameters carry source and status labels, and assumptions are stated openly. Field Shift supports, not replaces, farmer judgment: it models water stress, not yield or income.
details:
Problem. Rainfed farmers in Solapur’s semi-arid Deccan face erratic monsoon rainfall. Choosing a rotation depends on soil depth, the date monsoon rain arrives, and moisture stored for rabi crops. CRIDA’s district plan shows about 68% of the district has shallow black soils. Existing tools rarely show how uncertain a comparison is.

Solution. Field Shift is a self-contained web tool with a precomputed engine. Farmers or advisers pick a soil depth, an existing rotation, and priorities. The tool shows each rotation’s water stress, planting-window risk, where the rain goes, and how robust each comparison is.

How it works.

  • Data: NASA POWER daily point data for a 55 km grid cell near Pandharpur in western Solapur district (17.68°N, 75.32°E), 1984–2025. 1984 is spin-up, and 1985–2025 (41 years) is evaluated.
  • Evapotranspiration: FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference ET, tested against FAO’s worked Example 18 and a hand calculation.
  • Water balance: a daily root-zone balance with FAO-56 crop coefficients, a two-stage bare-soil evaporation model, and optional runoff. Rainfall equals crop ET, soil evaporation, losses, and storage change, with closure under 1e-6 mm.
  • Rotations: (R1) fallow then rabi sorghum, (R2) sole pigeonpea, (R3) pearl millet then chickpea.
  • Soils: shallow 0.20 m, medium 0.375 m, deep 1.0 m, from CRIDA depth classes, with an assumed available water of 190 mm/m.
  • Sowing: kharif crops sow at the first 3-day rainfall of at least 25 mm inside the CRIDA window (an assumed trigger). Rabi crops sow when stored moisture reaches 40% of capacity.
  • Two views of a missed planting window: one assumes late planting always works, and the other treats a missed window as total loss. They are optimistic and pessimistic bounds.
  • Uncertainty: 500 Monte Carlo draws over assumed (not measured) ranges for water capacity, sowing date, rain trigger, runoff, humidity method, evaporation settings, crop coefficients, and cultivar duration. The output is how often each ordering holds, not a probability of real outcomes.
  • Extras: a season calendar of soil water, ET₀ trend tests (Mann-Kendall, Theil-Sen, Pettitt), and parameter-source labels.

Findings so far [verify against docs/key-results.md]: soil depth dominates the results. When late planting always works, pigeon pea and millet-chickpea show lower mean deficit than fallow-sorghum in 95% to 98% of draws on deep soil, and 100% on medium and shallow soils. When a missed window counts as total loss, on deep soil fallow-sorghum is lower in about 71% and 65% of draws, while on medium and shallow soils the alternatives stay lower in 88% to 100%.

Tools. JavaScript on Node.js with no runtime dependencies, node:test (55 tests), static HTML/CSS/JS with inline SVG, git. Statistical tests are our own implementations, hand-checked against a published textbook benchmark.

Creativity. The distinctive features are showing when the tool cannot separate options, stating both missed-planting treatments openly, and labelling every parameter as cited, proxy, assumption, or pending. We make no claim of being the only tool that does this.

Benefits and intended impact. The tool is meant to help extension officers and farmers frame rotation discussions, see which options are plausible at which soil depth, and see where planting risk and bare-field periods fall. The impact is potential and has not been field-tested.

Limitations and future work.

  • The reanalysis grid is 55 km and gridded rainfall smooths storm peaks.
  • It models water stress, not yield, income, or markets.
  • No farmer or expert has validated it.
  • Soil health and pest cycles are qualitative: crop family and legume flags only.
  • Early-season crop evaporation uses a fixed initial coefficient, and fallow is modelled as bare soil.
  • Next steps: expert review with local extension (KVK), additional NASA products (SMAP, GPM, MODIS), more districts, and a dual-coefficient crop evaporation model.
